routes.description: Establish that libertarian sourcehood remains coherent under non-causal determination and that Bradleyan idealism accommodates agency, normativity, feeling, and inquiry without reducing reality to natural-scientific description.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by distinguishing logical determination from causal constraint, preserving meaningful alternatives and agential influence, and showing that Bradleyan idealism explains experiential and normative dimensions that reductive naturalism or pragmatic reconstruction leaves incomplete.

motionBridge.description: Show that libertarian agency joined to Bradleyan idealism answers determinist and naturalist pressures more comprehensively than compatibilist pragmatism.

centralBridges.description: Establish agential sourcehood and alternative possibility without requiring an objectively branching future or confusing logical implication with causal control.
Explain how reasoning and deliberation remain answerable to normative standards rather than becoming merely compelled psychological sequences.
Show why an adequate metaphysics must integrate scientific truth with agency, feeling, value, and experience instead of treating scientific description as exhaustive.
Ground the intelligibility and direction of inquiry in a real idealist completion joining knower and known, not solely in a useful regulative practice.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Demonstrate that indeterminacy, top-down constraint, or level-relative explanation can make libertarian alternatives coherent even within physicalist models.
Specify experiential, operational, and intellectual constraints that prevent idealist truth from becoming arbitrary or voluntarily constructed.

routes.description: Establish that non-causal determinism preserves the practical distinctions constituting free agency and that naturalistically acceptable, experience-centered pragmatism captures inquiry and progress without Bradleyan metaphysical commitments.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by showing that fixed laws and past conditions still pressure libertarian alternatives, that functional freedom supports deliberative and responsibility practices, and that pragmatic standards explain experience and inquiry without requiring an independently real absolute.

motionBridge.description: Show that compatibilist pragmatism answers the relevant determinist and naturalist pressures without the additional modal and metaphysical commitments of libertarian idealism.

centralBridges.description: Maintain the fixed-past challenge by distinguishing broad possible-world variation from the ability to act otherwise with the actual past and laws held fixed.
Define freedom through action-guiding distinctions involving reasons-responsiveness, coercion, prediction, incentives, praise, and blame under determinism.
Account for experience as inquiry's subject matter and physical objects as experiential models without inferring anti-naturalism or conscious control of reality.
Supply constrained standards for intellectual, moral, and aesthetic progress while testing whether a real Bradleyan absolute adds necessary explanation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Separate predictability from causal puppeteering while identifying the pressure complete external predictability places on libertarian branching.
Test whether an inaccessible unstructured feeling can support Bradleyan metaphysics when reflective perception is already categorically structured.

sections.title: Determinism, Alternative Possibilities, and Sourcehood
sections.rationale: This issue contains the principal modal clash over fixed pasts and laws, branching possibilities, logical determination, causal control, and whether agents can remain genuine sources.

sections.title: Normative Reasoning and Practical Freedom
sections.rationale: This issue connects the alleged self-undermining consequences of compelled reasoning with the compatibilist account of freedom through deliberation, responsibility, and socially useful distinctions.

sections.title: Naturalism, Reduction, and Experience
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether scientific explanation exhausts reality or whether experience, agency, feeling, morality, and aesthetics require the broader resources claimed for Bradleyan idealism.

sections.title: Idealist Truth, Feeling, and Perceptual Structure
sections.rationale: This issue tests how idealism constrains truth, whether precognitive feeling can ground thought, and whether unavoidable categorization supports or pressures Bradley's account of experience.

sections.title: The Absolute, Inquiry, and Pragmatic Standards
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether inquiry presupposes a genuinely real idealist completion or only a regulative commitment to progress, and what standards prevent either reductionism or unrestricted metaphysical admission.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Causal determinism threatens rational normativity because beliefs and inferences that are merely caused cannot remain answerable to independent standards of correct reasoning.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn begins with Hawkins accepting Folley's question and develops a sustained first-person response about determinism and normativity.

response.rationale: This is a constructive statement of the pro side's central normativity challenge and therefore has no earlier opposing target to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly states a central challenge and gives its self-defeat consequence, though the key bridge remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The thesis is recoverable, but the move shifts quickly from causal determination to beliefs being merely caused without specifying which accounts of rational answerability are excluded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The self-defeat conclusion is stronger than the supplied premise because causal production alone is not shown to eliminate truth-sensitive or norm-governed inference.

charity.alternative: A determinist can treat causal reasoning processes as truth-sensitive and responsive to logical norms.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move must show why causal realization precludes normative answerability rather than merely accompanying it.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference depends on an unsupported transition from being causally produced to being unable to answer to independent rational standards.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt invokes a recognized self-defeat line but supplies neither a developed warrant nor comparison with truth-tracking deterministic accounts.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable pro normativity bridge and states the consequence for rational endorsement of determinism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The determinist alternative is not seriously addressed, and the decisive incompatibility between causation and normative status remains asserted.

moves.evidenceBasis: Hawkins distinguishes correct or ought-governed reasoning from merely actual reasoning and says causal determinism would make belief in determinism itself merely caused.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Logical and mathematical relations provide mind-independent standards for how agents ought to reason, preserving a distinction between valid inference and psychologically caused thought.
moves.attributionBasis: After Folley requests a step-by-step account, Hawkins gives the historical and philosophical explanation in a clearly bounded response turn.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the positive standards component of the pro normativity route and has no earlier opposing target requiring response.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it explicitly identifies mind-independent logical relations as success criteria for reasoning, with only the metaphysical bridge compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast between psychological reasoning and independent logical principles is stable, although the precise sense of mind independence is left implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The need for standards beyond descriptions of actual psychology is well motivated, but their full mind-independent metaphysical status is not uniquely established.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The descriptive-versus-normative distinction supports independent standards, though the move leaves one bounded bridge from objectivity to mind independence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual contrast is specific and intelligible, but competing naturalistic accounts of logical normativity are not examined.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It supplies the positive standard needed by the pro central normativity bridge rather than merely repeating the self-defeat objection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move primarily develops its own positive account and does not materially interpret a live opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Hawkins says actual human reasoning must be distinguished from logical principles and that truth relations independent of human psychology set reasoning's success criteria.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Time-symmetric physical equations establish mathematical interconnection but do not establish that temporally prior states causally constrain or force later choices.
moves.attributionBasis: Hawkins continues his answer by marking a second issue, then develops the time-asymmetry and causation argument through its explicit conclusion.

response.rationale: This constructive move establishes the pro route's causal-versus-mathematical distinction and has no earlier opposing locked move to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it provides a pertinent physical analogy, but the conclusion about choice and sourcehood requires an additional modal bridge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction is recoverable, but time symmetry, causal explanation, constraint, and forcing are not fully separated across physical and agential contexts.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Reversibility supports denying a simple temporal forcing picture, but it does not by itself establish that fixed equations leave agential alternatives open.

charity.alternative: Time-symmetric laws can still uniquely relate complete states without assigning a privileged causal direction.
charity.decisiveQualification: Absence of forward causal forcing does not itself establish multiple futures with the same laws and state.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument usefully separates causal direction from equation-based determination but leaves a material bridge from non-forcing to libertarian sourcehood.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Reversible differential equations are a relevant example, yet their implications for agency and alternative possibility are not independently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central sourcehood bridge by attacking the identification of temporal determination with causal control.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes mathematical interconnection but does not fully handle the determinist's strongest uniqueness claim.

moves.evidenceBasis: Hawkins notes that Newtonian differential equations can be worked from past to future and backward, challenging a privileged past-to-future forcing interpretation.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: Even without causal necessitation, fixed laws and a fixed physical state that uniquely determine later states undermine libertarian branching alternatives.
moves.attributionBasis: Folley identifies the determinist audience's response, develops the branching-track model, and closes with a direct challenge to Hawkins.

components.text: Whether denying temporally directed causal forcing preserves the multiple alternatives required by libertarian freedom.

response.rationale: Folley accepts that determination need not be causal but argues that fixed laws and a fixed state still yield a unique track, directly contacting the decisive modal implication.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly targets the inference from non-causal determination to preserved branching and supplies a distinct uniqueness challenge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move consistently distinguishes causal necessitation from unique determination and specifies the fixed-state, fixed-law conditions of its branching challenge.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is framed as pressure on a branching picture rather than a complete refutation, matching the predictive and unique-track warrant supplied.

charity.alternative: Libertarian sourcehood might not require an objectively branching temporal structure.
charity.decisiveQualification: Folley's objection is decisive only against accounts requiring multiple continuations from the same fixed state and laws.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The fixed-state and fixed-law uniqueness premise coherently pressures branching even after causal direction is removed, with its target appropriately bounded.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The train-track and perfect-prediction model concretely supports the challenge, though the physical uniqueness premise is assumed rather than demonstrated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the con central fixed-past bridge by preserving determinist pressure under a non-causal formulation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly confines its objection to the branching-track target and does not equate predictability with causal puppeteering.

moves.evidenceBasis: Folley argues that fixing laws and physical states permits perfect prediction in either temporal direction and still eliminates multiple branching tracks.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Libertarian freedom requires both agential sourcehood and alternative possibility, but the relevant alternatives can exist across possible worlds without an objectively branching future.
moves.attributionBasis: Hawkins explicitly turns from the cited physicalist theory to his own libertarian position and develops it continuously through the possible-world conclusion.

components.text: Whether libertarian alternative possibility requires multiple objectively branching futures from one wholly fixed state.
Whether agential sourcehood remains available when physical determination is non-causal.

response.rationale: Hawkins answers by separating sourcehood from an objectively branching future and locating alternatives across relevant possible worlds, contacting both stated demands.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly rejects the branching requirement and supplies an alternative modal account, though its fixed-feature criterion remains incomplete.

precisionFindings.rationale: Sourcehood and possible-world alternatives are recoverable, but the set of relevant features held fixed is left flexible and partly unsettled.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents a possible libertarian account rather than claiming a decisive refutation, which fits its partly specified modal proposal.

charity.alternative: The consequence argument asks about alternatives with the actual past and laws fixed, not merely alternatives somewhere in modal space.
charity.decisiveQualification: A relevant-world account must justify which actual features may vary without trivializing the ability to do otherwise.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Separating sourcehood from objective branching is coherent, but the unspecified relevance relation leaves a material modal bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The possible-world proposal is intelligible but receives limited defense for why its selected variations constitute libertarian rather than broad modal ability.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the indispensable pro sourcehood bridge by supplying both source and alternative-possibility components.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes the holding-fixed question but does not fully answer the strongest fixed-past formulation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Hawkins says alternative possibility depends on which features are relevantly held fixed and contends that alternatives exist without an objectively branching future.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: Possible worlds with different pasts establish a broader ability to do otherwise than the consequence argument tests, which holds the actual past and laws fixed.
moves.attributionBasis: Folley carefully restates Hawkins's epistemic or modal account before contrasting it with the fixed-past scope of the consequence argument.

components.text: Whether possible-world alternatives with variable pasts answer the ability-to-do-otherwise demand posed by the consequence argument.

response.rationale: Folley diagnoses a scope difference between broad modal variation and worlds holding the actual past and laws fixed, then states why the former does not answer the latter.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it precisely identifies the quantifier-domain mismatch and its consequence for the claimed alternative possibility.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move explicitly distinguishes two scopes of ability and identifies exactly which past and laws are allowed to vary in each.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Given the stated difference in modal domains, the conclusion that they answer different questions follows without an omitted uncertainty caveat.

charity.alternative: Quantifying over worlds with different pasts is a legitimate broader account of an agent's ability.
charity.decisiveQualification: Its legitimacy does not make it responsive to the narrower consequence argument holding the actual past and laws fixed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The modal-scope diagnosis is explicit, internally consistent, and directly resolves the ambiguity in what is held fixed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The warrant is conceptual and specifically explained through contrasting possible-world domains, with only deeper defense of the consequence argument omitted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the con fixed-past bridge's indispensable distinction rather than offering merely adjacent determinist pressure.

representationalCharity.rationale: Folley expressly grants the broader usage's legitimacy before isolating the narrower demand, handling the strongest interpretation fairly.

moves.evidenceBasis: Folley grants that varying past and future across possible worlds is legitimate but contrasts it with the consequence argument's fixed actual past and laws.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: Non-causal determinism provides a basis for compatibilism because complete predictability need not amount to causal puppeteering or compulsion.
moves.attributionBasis: A marked Folley turn introduces his own compatibilist position and develops it continuously through the discussion of Laplace's demon and predictability.

response.rationale: This is a constructive presentation of non-causal compatibilism and therefore has no selected earlier opposing target to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it identifies a promising basis for compatibilism, although the functional account is only introduced rather than completed here.

precisionFindings.rationale: The predictability-versus-puppeteering contrast is clear, but what makes the position specifically compatibilist rather than merely non-causal remains compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Folley's tentative claim that non-causal determinism may provide a stronger basis matches the exploratory support offered.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Separating predictability from causal compulsion is coherent, but a material bridge to freedom and responsibility remains undeveloped in this move.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Laplacean predictability supplies a useful illustration, while the positive sufficiency of non-puppeteering for compatibilism is largely asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally advances the con functional-freedom route by removing causal puppeteering as a necessary feature of determination.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops Folley's own compatibilist basis and does not materially characterize an opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Folley presents non-causal determinism as stronger than causal determinism for compatibilism and separates complete predictability from being causally puppeteered.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: Free will is functionally constituted by distinctions used to guide incentives, prediction, praise, and blame, which remain meaningful in a deterministic society.
moves.attributionBasis: Folley's uninterrupted extended turn develops a thought experiment about deterministic societies, pathological behavior, coercion, prediction, and the practical work performed by freedom concepts.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the practical-content account of compatibilist freedom and has no earlier opposing target requiring response.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it gives explicit action-guiding functions for freedom language and connects them to deterministic social practices.

precisionFindings.rationale: The functional question and the roles of prediction, incentives, praise, blame, and coercion are stated with stable practical scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move offers a functional analysis as a viable account, not as a demonstrated exhaustive definition, matching its thought-experimental support.

charity.alternative: Libertarians may agree these practices are useful while denying that usefulness constitutes metaphysical freedom.
charity.decisiveQualification: A functional account must distinguish explaining the use of freedom concepts from establishing that the agent has the disputed control.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from stable practical distinctions to a functional freedom concept is clear, with one bounded bridge concerning constitutive sufficiency.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The deterministic-society thought experiment and concrete social functions provide specific support, though rival sourcehood accounts are not compared fully.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies nearly every stated component of the con central functional-freedom bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops the practical alternative strongly but does not fully address the metaphysical insufficiency objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: Folley asks what free will does and argues that it structures prediction, coercion distinctions, incentives, praise, and blame even in deterministic societies.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Bradleyan idealism accepts scientific truths while denying that they exhaust reality, requiring metaphysics also to integrate agential, moral, aesthetic, religious, and felt experience.
moves.attributionBasis: Following Folley's direct invitation, Hawkins gives a sustained exposition of Bradley and British idealism, with stable first-person framing and no competing speaker turn until the endpoint.

components.text: Whether a practical functional account exhausts the agential and evaluative phenomena an adequate metaphysics must integrate.
Whether removing causal puppeteering provides a complete account of agency rather than one compatible component.

response.rationale: Hawkins replaces a narrowly functional demand with a broader adequacy test and justifies it by identifying moral, aesthetic, religious, scientific, and agential domains needing integration.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within justified reframes, it preserves the issue of explaining agency while broadening the adequacy criterion, though it does not directly disprove functional compatibilism.

precisionFindings.rationale: The acceptance of scientific truth and denial of scientific exhaustiveness are clearly distinguished, with the additional experiential domains enumerated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The need to integrate the listed domains is plausible, but the move does not establish that Bradleyan metaphysics is uniquely required to do so.

charity.alternative: Compatibilist pragmatism can treat moral, aesthetic, and agential practices as real without making science metaphysically exhaustive.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing that science abstracts from values does not show that pragmatism cannot integrate them.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The non-exhaustion inference is coherent if the listed domains resist scientific reduction, but that antecedent is only partly defended.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move provides representative domains and Bradley's integrative aim, while comparative evidence against nonreductive pragmatism remains compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the pro central idealist-completeness bridge by specifying what scientific description allegedly leaves out.

representationalCharity.rationale: The broader target is legitimate, but the move underdevelops the strongest nonreductive naturalist alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Hawkins describes British idealism as accepting science while seeking a coherent account integrating agency and aesthetic, moral, religious, and scientific engagement.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Reality is richer than intellectual thought because feeling and volition precede systematic reflection, while science deliberately abstracts from agential, ethical, and aesthetic value.
moves.attributionBasis: Hawkins explicitly introduces Bradley's rejection of thought-centered Hegelian idealism and carries the same exposition through its contrast with contemporary analytic idealisms.

response.rationale: This constructive move develops Bradley's positive non-intellectualist metaphysics and has no earlier opposing target selected for response.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it identifies feeling and volition as omitted dimensions and explains science's abstraction, though the metaphysical conclusion remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast with intellectual abstraction is recoverable, but feeling, volition, value, and reality's richness are grouped without fully specified relations.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Science's designed abstraction from value supports non-exhaustiveness, but the stronger claim that feeling precedes and grounds systematic thought receives limited support here.

charity.alternative: Science can abstract from value methodologically without denying that value and agency are natural features of reality.
charity.decisiveQualification: Methodological omission does not alone entail metaphysical incompleteness of naturalism.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument clearly identifies excluded subject matter, but a material bridge remains from methodological abstraction to the required idealist ontology.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Ethical, aesthetic, and agential examples are concrete, though the claims about precognitive priority and metaphysical consequence remain mainly expository.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports idealist completeness by identifying feeling, volition, and value as dimensions an intellectual system allegedly cannot exhaust.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move treats scientific abstraction as significant but does not fully engage the methodological-versus-metaphysical distinction.

moves.evidenceBasis: Hawkins argues that science is an intellectual abstraction which leaves agential, ethical, aesthetic, pleasurable, and volitional value untouched by design.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: An experience-centered idealism can remain naturalistically acceptable by treating experience as inquiry's subject matter and physical objects as useful models of experience.
moves.attributionBasis: The marked Folley turn uses Carnap, phenomenalism, Hume, and the Vienna Circle to articulate his own experience-first but naturalistic position before Hawkins resumes.

components.text: Whether taking experience as inquiry's subject matter requires Bradleyan anti-naturalist metaphysical commitments.
Whether acknowledging experience and abstraction requires mysterious mental substance or an expanded idealist ontology.

response.rationale: Folley preserves the demand to center experience but reframes idealism as modeling experience naturalistically, thereby offering a less metaphysically demanding alternative.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within justified reframes, it directly preserves experiential subject matter and explains the replacement model, though it only partly addresses value and volition.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between mental substance claims and experience-first inquiry is stable, and physical objects are clearly characterized as experiential models.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The position is offered as a naturalistically acceptable possibility, appropriately matching the conceptual examples and historical references supplied.

charity.alternative: Bradleyan idealism claims not only that inquiry concerns experience but that feeling, value, and volition require integration beyond naturalistic models.
charity.decisiveQualification: An experience-first model must show it captures those dimensions rather than merely redescribing perceptual subject matter.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Treating physical objects as useful models of experience coherently avoids an inference to mysterious mental stuff, with one bounded completeness gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Carnapian, phenomenalist, and Humean examples support conceptual viability, but the account's treatment of normativity and value is not developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the con central naturalistic-idealism bridge by explaining experience-first inquiry without anti-naturalist commitments.

representationalCharity.rationale: Folley's alternative fairly answers the experience component but only partially handles the broader integrative aspiration.

moves.evidenceBasis: Folley distinguishes mental-substance idealism from a naturalistically acceptable view in which inquiry organizes experience and physical objects model it.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: Although idealism need not imply voluntary control over reality, Bradley's unstructured felt real is pressured by the categorization already built into accessible perception.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn uses the host's first-person pragmatist framing and ends by directly asking how Bradley handles perceptual categorization.

components.text: Whether precognitive or non-intellectual feeling can serve as metaphysical support when accessible perception is already categorized.
Whether idealism entails voluntary control of experienced reality.

response.rationale: Folley grants that idealism need not imply voluntary control, then directly questions how an unstructured felt real can be supported through categorically structured perception.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly grants one clarification and presses the decisive epistemic problem for precognitive feeling.

precisionFindings.rationale: The categorization challenge is clear, though 'the real,' felt experience, and accessible perception retain some terminological compression.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents categorization as a concern and question rather than claiming it conclusively refutes Bradley, fitting its limited warrant.

charity.alternative: Bradley may treat unstructured feeling as a transcendental foundation rather than an object available in reflective perception.
charity.decisiveQualification: Its inaccessibility still raises the question of what warrants assigning it the claimed structureless foundational role.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from unavoidable accessible categorization to pressure on evidential access to unstructured feeling is careful and appropriately limited.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The phenomenological observation is specific, but the universality of categorization and its implications for Bradley are not extensively defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the con subsidiary perceptual-structure bridge but does not independently complete a central naturalist burden.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move grants idealism's non-voluntarist form and targets the strongest residual epistemic problem without caricature.

moves.evidenceBasis: Folley rejects the idea that idealism implies voluntary control and asks how Bradley's felt real can be accessed when perception already categorizes experience.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Bradleyan truth combines operational coherence with constraints from felt reality and intellectual satisfaction, so false claims encounter practical failure rather than becoming true by choice.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly answers Folley's question, interprets Bradley and Russell, and presents the position as a pragmatism-plus conception.

components.text: Whether Bradleyan idealism has reality-based constraints preventing truth from becoming arbitrary or voluntarily chosen.
Whether operational success alone exhausts the constraints governing idealist truth.

response.rationale: Hawkins answers the constraint concern through practical operation, felt encounter, and intellectual satisfaction, while separating truth from voluntary construction.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it directly supplies multiple constraints, although it only indirectly addresses the distinct categorization problem.

precisionFindings.rationale: The three constraints are identifiable, but felt encounter and intellectual satisfaction are not fully specified as independent truth conditions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The account is presented as pragmatism plus additional constraints rather than as a fully proven truth theory, matching its expository support.

charity.alternative: Operational coherence and satisfaction may constrain belief without guaranteeing correspondence to an independent reality.
charity.decisiveQualification: The account must explain how felt encounter discriminates truth from stable but mistaken coherence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Combining operational, felt, and intellectual constraints coherently blocks simple voluntarism, though their joint truth-making role remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Practical failure provides a concrete check, while felt and intellectual constraints are asserted without representative tests or rival comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly and strongly supports the pro subsidiary truth-constraint bridge but does not by itself establish idealist completeness.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move supplies genuine constraints but does not resolve the strongest discrimination objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: Hawkins characterizes Bradley's truth as pragmatism plus practical operation, felt encounter with reality, and intellectual satisfaction, allowing false claims to fail.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Although reflective agents cannot recover wholly unstructured experience, precognitive feeling remains thought's foundation and is ultimately integrated with thought and volition in the absolute.
moves.attributionBasis: The same answering speaker explicitly takes up the second question, repeatedly names Bradley, and develops the idealist account through the absolute.

components.text: Whether the inaccessibility of wholly unstructured experience defeats its proposed foundational role in thought.
How reflective categorization relates to precognitive feeling in Bradley's account.

response.rationale: Hawkins concedes that reflective agents never encounter the raw precognitive state but answers that it persists as thought's foundation and is integrated in the absolute.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it directly acknowledges the access problem and states Bradley's answer, though it does not independently warrant the foundational inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The concession and foundational thesis are clear, but foundation, persistence, and ultimate integration shift between phenomenological and metaphysical scopes.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The explicit concession improves calibration, but inaccessible feeling's foundational and absolute integration roles exceed the evidence supplied.

charity.alternative: If all reportable experience is categorized, unstructured feeling may be a theoretical posit rather than an experienced foundation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Bradley's concession of inaccessibility requires an independent warrant for the posit's foundational status.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The concession is consistent with a theoretical foundation, yet a material epistemic bridge remains from inaccessible feeling to its claimed role.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Reflective experience and Bradley's admission are specifically described, but evidence for persistence and integration in the absolute is largely doctrinal assertion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the con subsidiary perceptual-structure challenge and clarifies the proposed relationship between feeling and thought.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection is squarely acknowledged, but the decisive warrant is answered mainly by restating Bradley's theory.

moves.evidenceBasis: Hawkins concedes that raw precognitive feeling is never encountered in judgment but says it remains the foundation of thought and is integrated with volition in the absolute.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: Bradley's absolute requires clarification between a regulative ideal that guides inquiry and an independently real endpoint whose existence adds a substantive metaphysical commitment.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn compares Bradley with C. S. Peirce in the host's pragmatist vocabulary and concludes with an explicit question about Bradley's certainty.

components.text: Whether Bradley's absolute is merely a regulative ideal or an independently real metaphysical completion.

response.rationale: Folley directly identifies the ambiguity between a Peircean regulative endpoint and an existent absolute and asks what substantive certainty Bradley claims.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it isolates the decisive ontological fork with an explicit comparison, though it poses rather than resolves the challenge.

precisionFindings.rationale: Regulative guidance, independent existence, attainability, and agnosticism are clearly differentiated throughout the question.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move asks for clarification instead of assuming either interpretation, exactly matching its comparative warrant.

charity.alternative: The absolute may be a real completion without being temporally reached or fully describable by present inquiry.
charity.decisiveQualification: Bradley still owes a reason to move from inquiry's direction to that completion's independent reality.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The regulative-versus-real distinction is explicit and exposes the exact additional premise required by the realist conclusion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Peircean comparison provides a concrete rival model, although the excerpt does not develop textual evidence about Bradley beyond Hawkins's presentation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the pro central absolute bridge by testing whether the asserted endpoint adds warranted metaphysical content.

representationalCharity.rationale: The question leaves room for both regulative and realist interpretations while pinpointing the extra commitment requiring defense.

moves.evidenceBasis: Folley contrasts Peirce's agnostic end-of-inquiry ideal with an absolute that exists independently and asks whether Bradley claims certainty about the latter.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: The normative drive toward fulfilled truth treats complete reality as more real than present partial understanding, so Bradley's absolute is not merely a convenient regulative fiction.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker calls the preceding question excellent, explicitly answers that Bradley is not agnostic, and supplies Bradley-specific reasons.

components.text: Whether Bradley has grounds for treating the absolute as real rather than merely a useful regulative fiction.

response.rationale: Hawkins explicitly answers that Bradley is not agnostic and argues from inquiry's normative orientation toward fuller truth to the greater reality of the whole.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it directly answers the ontological question and supplies a Bradley-specific inference, even though that inference remains disputable.

precisionFindings.rationale: The regulative-fiction contrast is clear, but 'more real' moves between normative superiority and ontological completion without full definition.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A normative drive toward completeness does not by itself necessitate an independently real completed whole, and that modal gap is not acknowledged.

charity.alternative: Inquiry can be normatively directed toward fuller truth without presupposing that a completed absolute independently exists.
charity.decisiveQualification: The norm of improvement establishes direction or evaluation, not necessarily an existent terminus.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The central inference equivocates between normative priority and ontological reality, leaving the indispensable realist bridge substantially unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The examples of truth, beauty, and goodness establish normative striving but provide weak warrant for an independently real absolute.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It squarely supports the pro central absolute bridge by supplying the explicit reason offered for realism about completion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply answers the alternative but largely converts normative orientation into ontology without meeting its decisive qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Hawkins says Bradley is not agnostic: inquiry's normative drive toward completed truth recognizes the whole as more real than present partial understanding.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Inquiry presupposes an intelligible attainable end, and idealism explains that intelligibility by joining knower and known within experience rather than positing wholly inaccessible independent reality.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker affirms Folley's analogy and then develops Bradley's idealist explanation, consistently referring to Bradley in an expository voice.

components.text: What idealism adds to the intelligibility of inquiry's endpoint beyond a merely regulative commitment.

response.rationale: Hawkins answers that idealism joins knower and known within an interactive experiential whole, making directed inquiry intelligible rather than aimed at wholly inaccessible reality.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it supplies a direct idealist explanation of intelligibility, though the step from direction to an attainable endpoint is incomplete.

precisionFindings.rationale: The knower-known relation is recoverable, but affecting the known, experiential unity, intelligibility, and attainability are not sharply distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The explanation is presented as Bradley's attraction rather than certainty, but directed movement alone only weakly supports a real attainable terminus.

charity.alternative: Pragmatic inquiry can be intelligible through fallible interaction with reality without knower and known belonging to a completed absolute.
charity.decisiveQualification: Interaction and direction do not uniquely imply metaphysical identity or a predetermined endpoint.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Joining knower and known can explain interaction, but the inference from directional inquiry to an intelligible attainable completion retains a material gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The experiential interaction claim is articulated, while the existence and attainability of the endpoint receive mainly suggestive metaphorical support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the pro central absolute bridge by explaining why idealism allegedly makes inquiry's completion intelligible.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move offers a positive idealist explanation but does not compare it adequately with the strongest fallibilist pragmatic account.

moves.evidenceBasis: Hawkins says knower and known are together, knowing affects what is known, and directed movement within this interaction appears to head toward an intelligible end.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: A defensible anti-reductionism requires pragmatic admission standards that avoid both scientistic exclusion and an unrestricted metaphysical free-for-all.
moves.attributionBasis: The host explicitly responds to the tension in Hawkins's answer, states his distance from scientism, and identifies the pragmatic maxim as his current approach.

components.text: Whether the desire for an inclusive metaphysics supplies standards warranting Bradley's additional commitments.
Whether normative direction licenses admission of a real absolute rather than a restrained pragmatic ideal.
How to avoid scientistic exclusion while retaining discriminating standards for broader metaphysical claims.

response.rationale: Folley accepts the anti-reductionist concern but insists on admission standards and proposes the pragmatic maxim while acknowledging the difficulty, contacting the decisive comparative demand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly addresses both over-exclusion and unrestricted admission, though the proposed pragmatic standard is not operationalized in detail.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two errors, need for standards, and tentative pragmatic criterion are clearly stated with stable scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Folley's repeated acknowledgment that selecting standards is difficult appropriately limits the force of his pragmatic proposal.

charity.alternative: Bradleyan metaphysics may claim disciplined experiential, practical, and intellectual constraints rather than unrestricted admission.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those constraints still require a criterion showing when they warrant a substantive absolute rather than merely permit it.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The balanced demand for nonreductive but discriminating standards is coherent, with one bounded gap in specifying how the pragmatic maxim decides cases.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The dilemma is clearly motivated, but the pragmatic maxim is named rather than applied to representative idealist commitments.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the con central pragmatic-standards bridge and tests the admission of the real absolute on the route's decisive issue.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move does not caricature idealism as a free-for-all; it frames unrestricted admission as one risk and acknowledges the shared need for standards.

moves.evidenceBasis: Folley rejects both scientistic exclusion and metaphysical free-for-all, says standards are necessary, and tentatively favors the pragmatic maxim while stressing the difficulty.
